claim: Chromosome 4q deletion is one of the most frequently detected genomic imbalance events in congenital heart disease (CHD) patients.
source: Chromosome 4q deletion is one of the most frequently detected genomic imbalance events in congenital heart disease (CHD) patients.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that is supported by established knowledge in the field of CHD genetics.

claim: A portion of CHD-associated 4q deletions without known CHD genes suggests unknown CHD genes within these intervals.
source: However, a portion of CHD-associated 4q deletions without known CHD genes suggests unknown CHD genes within these intervals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that some 4q deletions associated with CHD do not contain known CHD genes.

claim: Knockdown of SORBS2 disrupted sarcomeric integrity of cardiomyocytes in human embryonic stem cell differentiation model.
source: Here, we have shown that knockdown of SORBS2, a 4q interval gene, disrupted sarcomeric integrity of cardiomyocytes and caused reduced cardiomyocyte number in human embryonic stem cell differentiation model.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the hESC differentiation experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Knockdown of SORBS2 caused reduced cardiomyocyte number in human embryonic stem cell differentiation model.
source: Here, we have shown that knockdown of SORBS2, a 4q interval gene, disrupted sarcomeric integrity of cardiomyocytes and caused reduced cardiomyocyte number in human embryonic stem cell differentiation model.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the hESC differentiation experiments shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: SORBS2 knockdown decreased expression of second heart field (SHF) marker genes.
source: Molecular analyses revealed decreased expression of second heart field (SHF) marker genes and impaired NOTCH and SHH signaling in SORBS2-knockdown cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1F-H.

claim: SORBS2 knockdown impaired NOTCH signaling.
source: Molecular analyses revealed decreased expression of second heart field (SHF) marker genes and impaired NOTCH and SHH signaling in SORBS2-knockdown cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data, western blot, and qPCR data shown in Figure 1K-N.

claim: SORBS2 knockdown impaired SHH signaling.
source: Molecular analyses revealed decreased expression of second heart field (SHF) marker genes and impaired NOTCH and SHH signaling in SORBS2-knockdown cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4G and Figure 1O.

claim: Exogenous SHH rescued SORBS2 knockdown-induced cardiomyocyte differentiation defects.
source: Exogenous SHH rescued SORBS2 knockdown-induced cardiomyocyte differentiation defects.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from rescue experiments shown in Figure 1O-Q.

claim: Sorbs2-/- mouse mutants had atrial septal hypoplasia/aplasia.
source: Sorbs2-/- mouse mutants had atrial septal hypoplasia/aplasia or double atrial septum (DAS) derived from impaired posterior SHF with a similar expression alteration.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis of Sorbs2-/- mouse hearts shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Sorbs2-/- mouse mutants had double atrial septum (DAS).
source: Sorbs2-/- mouse mutants had atrial septal hypoplasia/aplasia or double atrial septum (DAS) derived from impaired posterior SHF with a similar expression alteration.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis of Sorbs2-/- mouse hearts shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Atrial septal defects in Sorbs2-/- mice are derived from impaired posterior SHF.
source: Sorbs2-/- mouse mutants had atrial septal hypoplasia/aplasia or double atrial septum (DAS) derived from impaired posterior SHF with a similar expression alteration.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis showing DMP malformation (Figure 2D) and molecular analysis showing decreased SHF marker expression (Figure 3).

claim: Rare SORBS2 variants were significantly enriched in a cohort of 300 CHD patients.
source: Rare SORBS2 variants were significantly enriched in a cohort of 300 CHD patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of targeted sequencing data shown in Figure 4B and Supplementary file 7.

claim: SORBS2 is a regulator of SHF development.
source: Our findings indicate that SORBS2 is a regulator of SHF development and its variants contribute to CHD pathogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence including in vitro differentiation data, mouse model data, and molecular analyses.

claim: SORBS2 variants contribute to CHD pathogenesis.
source: Our findings indicate that SORBS2 is a regulator of SHF development and its variants contribute to CHD pathogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by the enrichment of rare SORBS2 variants in CHD patients and functional studies.

claim: The presence of DAS in Sorbs2-/- hearts reveals the first molecular etiology of this rare anomaly linked to paradoxical thromboembolism.
source: The presence of DAS in Sorbs2-/- hearts reveals the first molecular etiology of this rare anomaly linked to paradoxical thromboembolism.
evidence: This claim is based on the observation of DAS in Sorbs2-/- mice and knowledge that DAS is linked to paradoxical thromboembolism.

claim: Patients with 4q deletion syndrome have a spectrum of clinical manifestations including craniofacial, cardiovascular, and gastrointestinal abnormalities, and mental and growth deficiencies.
source: Patients have a spectrum of clinical manifestations including craniofacial, cardiovascular, and gastrointestinal abnormalities, and mental and growth deficiencies (Strehle and Bantock, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Congenital heart disease (CHD) is a common defect seen in about half of the 4q deletion patients.
source: Congenital heart disease (CHD) is a common defect seen in about half of the 4q deletion patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: A previous study narrowed the cardiovascular critical region to 4q32.2–q34.3, which contains TLL1, HPGD, and HAND2 genes.
source: A previous study narrowed the cardiovascular critical region to 4q32.2–q34.3, which contains TLL1, HPGD, and HAND2 genes (Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Over-represented right-sided CHDs in 4q deletion syndrome patients suggest that HAND2, an essential regulator of the second heart field (SHF), is mainly responsible for the CHD phenotype.
source: Over-represented right-sided CHDs in 4q deletion syndrome patients suggest that HAND2, an essential regulator of the second heart field (SHF), is mainly responsible for the CHD phenotype (Xu et al., 2012; Huang et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and inference from the observation of right-sided CHDs.

claim: A part of terminal 4q deletions with CHDs does not cover HAND2.
source: However, a part of terminal 4q deletions with CHDs that we and others have discovered does not cover HAND2(Geng et al., 2014; Strehle et al., 2012; Tsai et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature including the authors' own work.

claim: SORBS2 within chromosomal 4q35.1 has been proposed as a candidate gene for CHD of terminal 4q deletion syndrome based on an unusual small interstitial deletion.
source: SORBS2 within chromosomal 4q35.1 has been proposed as a candidate gene for CHD of terminal 4q deletion syndrome based on an unusual small interstitial deletion (Strehle et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: SORBS2 knockdown achieved approximately 40% of wild-type expression level.
source: We used two different short hairpin RNAs (shRNAs) to knock down SORBS2, and similar knockdown efficiencies (~40% of wild-type expression level) were achieved (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: SORBS2 knockdown did not affect clone morphology of human embryonic stem cells.
source: SORBS2 knockdown did not affect clone morphology, pluripotency marker expression, and apoptosis of human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-1F.

claim: SORBS2 knockdown did not affect pluripotency marker expression of human embryonic stem cells.
source: SORBS2 knockdown did not affect clone morphology, pluripotency marker expression, and apoptosis of human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-1F.

claim: SORBS2 knockdown did not affect apoptosis of human embryonic stem cells.
source: SORBS2 knockdown did not affect clone morphology, pluripotency marker expression, and apoptosis of human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Spontaneous beating started to appear at differentiation day 8 (D8) in both control and SORBS2-knockdown cells.
source: After in vitro cardiac differentiation (Burridge et al., 2014; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), spontaneous beating started to appear at differentiation day 8 (D8) in both control and SORBS2-knockdown cells, but differentiated SORBS2-knockdown cardiomyocytes contracted much weaker (Videos 1–3).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation of cell cultures and videos.

claim: Differentiated SORBS2-knockdown cardiomyocytes contracted much weaker than control cells.
source: After in vitro cardiac differentiation (Burridge et al., 2014; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), spontaneous beating started to appear at differentiation day 8 (D8) in both control and SORBS2-knockdown cells, but differentiated SORBS2-knockdown cardiomyocytes contracted much weaker (Videos 1–3).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation of cell cultures shown in Videos 1-3.

claim: The cardiomyocyte differentiation efficiency (the proportion of cTnT+ cells) was significantly decreased in SORBS2-knockdown group at D15.
source: The cardiomyocyte differentiation efficiency (the proportion of cTnT+ cells) was significantly decreased in SORBS2-knockdown group at D15 (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: SORBS2 is a structural component of sarcomeric Z-line.
source: Since SORBS2 is a structural component of sarcomeric Z-line and cardiomyopathy gene (Ding et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020; Sanger et al., 2010), we examined the myofibril structure of differentiated cardiomyocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SORBS2 is a cardiomyopathy gene.
source: Since SORBS2 is a structural component of sarcomeric Z-line and cardiomyopathy gene (Ding et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020; Sanger et al., 2010), we examined the myofibril structure of differentiated cardiomyocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Most cardiomyocytes in SORBS2-knockdown group presented a round or oval shape instead of polygonal or spindle-like outlines in control group.
source: Most cardiomyocytes in SORBS2-knockdown group presented a round or oval shape instead of polygonal or spindle-like outlines in control group, and a close lookup indicated that sarcomeric structure in cells with abnormal shapes was disrupted (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Sarcomeric structure in SORBS2-knockdown cells with abnormal shapes was disrupted.
source: Most cardiomyocytes in SORBS2-knockdown group presented a round or oval shape instead of polygonal or spindle-like outlines in control group, and a close lookup indicated that sarcomeric structure in cells with abnormal shapes was disrupted (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The percentage of cardiomyocytes with well-organized sarcomeres and a normal shape was much lower in SORBS2-knockdown group.
source: The percentage of cardiomyocytes with well-organized sarcomeres and a normal shape was much lower in SORBS2-knockdown group (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Disrupted sarcomeric structures in SORBS2-knockdown cardiomyocytes were present in transmission electron microscopy analysis.
source: Disrupted sarcomeric structures in SORBS2-knockdown cardiomyocytes were also present in transmission electron microscopy analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The expression of sarcomeric genes TNNT2, MYL7, MYH6, and MYH7 was significantly decreased in SORBS2-knockdown cells.
source: The expression of sarcomeric genes TNNT2, MYL7, MYH6, and MYH7 was significantly decreased (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B–3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B-3E.

claim: The dominant type of cardiomyocytes is ventricular-like in both control and SORBS2-knockdown groups.
source: The dominant type of cardiomyocytes is ventricular-like in both control and SORBS2-knockdown groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3F.

claim: Action potential parameters of ventricular-like cells showed no difference between control and SORBS2-knockdown groups.
source: Statistical analyses on action potential parameters of ventricular-like cells, including average action potential (AP) duration at 90% repolarization, average AP frequency, peak amplitude, and resting potential, showed no difference between two groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 3G–3J).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3G-3J.

claim: SORBS2 was up-regulated at cardiac progenitor stage D5 after a transient absence at mesodermal cell stage (D2-D3).
source: Expression dynamics showed that SORBS2 was up-regulated at cardiac progenitor stage D5 after a transient absence at mesodermal cell stage (D2-D3) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: SORBS2-knockdown group disrupted the expression of cardiac progenitor markers.
source: Consistently, SORBS2-knockdown group disrupted the expression of cardiac progenitor markers, whereas mesodermal markers remained unchanged (Figure 1F–H, Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1F-H and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A-4E.

claim: Mesodermal markers remained unchanged in SORBS2-knockdown cells.
source: Consistently, SORBS2-knockdown group disrupted the expression of cardiac progenitor markers, whereas mesodermal markers remained unchanged (Figure 1F–H, Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A-4B.

claim: There are two sets of molecularly distinct cardiac progenitors during mammalian heart development, referred to as the first and second heart fields (FHF and SHF).
source: There are two sets of molecularly distinct cardiac progenitors during mammalian heart development, referred to as the first and second heart fields (FHF and SHF), which contribute to distinct anatomical structures of the heart (Srivastava, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: FHF and SHF contribute to distinct anatomical structures of the heart.
source: There are two sets of molecularly distinct cardiac progenitors during mammalian heart development, referred to as the first and second heart fields (FHF and SHF), which contribute to distinct anatomical structures of the heart (Srivastava, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: Expression of FHF markers (TBX5, HCN4, HAND1) was significantly increased in SORBS2-knockdown cells.
source: Interestingly, we found significantly increased expression of FHF markers (TBX5, HCN4, HAND1) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C–4E) while significantly decreased expression of SHF markers (TBX1, ISL1, MEF2C) in SORBS2-knockdown cells (Figure 1F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C-4E.

claim: Expression of SHF markers (TBX1, ISL1, MEF2C) was significantly decreased in SORBS2-knockdown cells.
source: Interestingly, we found significantly increased expression of FHF markers (TBX5, HCN4, HAND1) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C–4E) while significantly decreased expression of SHF markers (TBX1, ISL1, MEF2C) in SORBS2-knockdown cells (Figure 1F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1F-H.

claim: SHF gives rise to cardiac outflow, right ventricle, and inflow.
source: SHF gives rise to cardiac outflow, right ventricle, and inflow (Kelly, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: Any defect in SHF-derived embryonic structures leads to CHDs commonly seen in 4q deletion syndrome.
source: Any defect in these embryonic structures leads to CHDs commonly seen in 4q deletion syndrome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the knowledge that SHF gives rise to structures commonly affected in 4q deletion syndrome.

claim: 160 genes were down-regulated and 104 genes were up-regulated in D5 SORBS2-knockdown cells using stringent threshold (padj <0.05, |log2(fold change)|>1).
source: Using a stringent threshold (padj <0.05, |log2(fold change)|>1), we selected out 160 down-regulated and 104 up-regulated genes for gene ontology (GO) analysis (Figure 1I, Supplementary file 1–2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1I and Supplementary files 1-2.

claim: Up-regulated genes in SORBS2-knockdown cells were enriched in biological processes like cell adhesion.
source: Results showed that the up-regulated genes were enriched in biological processes like cell adhesion and so on (Figure 1J), which might be a compensatory reaction to reduced SORBS2 as a cytoskeleton component.
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Up-regulation of cell adhesion genes might be a compensatory reaction to reduced SORBS2 as a cytoskeleton component.
source: Results showed that the up-regulated genes were enriched in biological processes like cell adhesion and so on (Figure 1J), which might be a compensatory reaction to reduced SORBS2 as a cytoskeleton component.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the GO analysis results.

claim: Down-regulated genes in SORBS2-knockdown cells were enriched in biological processes like heart development.
source: The down-regulated genes were enriched in biological processes like heart development and so on (Figure 1K), suggesting that SORBS2 positively regulates cardiac development.
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 1K.

claim: SORBS2 positively regulates cardiac development.
source: The down-regulated genes were enriched in biological processes like heart development and so on (Figure 1K), suggesting that SORBS2 positively regulates cardiac development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the GO analysis showing enrichment of heart development genes among down-regulated genes.

claim: NOTCH signaling pathway was in the down-regulated gene list in SORBS2-knockdown cells.
source: Particularly, we noted the NOTCH signaling pathway in the down-regulated list (Figure 1K–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis and heatmap shown in Figure 1K-L.

claim: NOTCH1 expression was not differentially expressed at RNA level in SORBS2-knockdown cells.
source: In contrast, we did not see differential expression for NOTCH1 in RNA-seq (Figure 1L), suggesting that the regulation of SORBS2 on NOTCH signaling might be through modulating protein level.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: The regulation of SORBS2 on NOTCH signaling might be through modulating protein level.
source: In contrast, we did not see differential expression for NOTCH1 in RNA-seq (Figure 1L), suggesting that the regulation of SORBS2 on NOTCH signaling might be through modulating protein level.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that NOTCH signaling is affected but NOTCH1 RNA is not changed.

claim: SORBS2 can interact with the non-receptor tyrosine kinase c-ABL as SH3 domain-containing adaptor.
source: SORBS2 can interact with the non-receptor tyrosine kinase c-ABL as SH3 domain-containing adaptor (Kioka et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The binding of SORBS2 to c-ABL triggers the recruitment of ubiquitin ligase CBL and leads to the ubiquitination of c-ABL.
source: The binding of SORBS2 to c-ABL triggers the recruitment of ubiquitin ligase CBL and leads to the ubiquitination of c-ABL (Soubeyran et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: c-ABL protein level was significantly elevated in SORBS2-knockdown cells.
source: Indeed, we noted that c-ABL protein level was significantly elevated in SORBS2-knockdown cells (Figure 1M).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1M.

claim: c-Abl can promote Notch endocytosis to modulate Notch signaling.
source: c-Abl can promote Notch endocytosis to modulate Notch signaling (Xiong et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: NOTCH1 protein level decreased significantly in SORBS2-knockdown cells.
source: Consistently, NOTCH1 protein level decreased significantly in SORBS2-knockdown cells (Figure 1N).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1N.

claim: Notch signaling is a well-known molecular mechanism enhancing cellular response to Shh.
source: Notch signaling is a well-known molecular mechanism enhancing cellular response to Shh (Stasiulewicz et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: The expression of SHH and SHH signaling targets, PTCH1 and GLI1, was reduced in SORBS2-knockdown cells.
source: We noted that the expression of SHH and SHH signaling targets, PTCH1 and GLI1, was also reduced in SORBS2-knockdown cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4G.

claim: Exogenous SHH activated PTCH1 and GLI1 expression in SORBS2-knockdown cells.
source: As expected, exogenous SHH activated PTCH1 and GLI1 expression (Figure 1O).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from rescue experiments shown in Figure 1O.

claim: Exogenous SHH up-regulated the expression of SHF markers ISL1 and MEF2C in D5 SORBS2-shRNA1 cells.
source: It also up-regulated the expression of SHF markers ISL1 and MEF2C in D5 SORBS2-shRNA1 cells (Figure 1O) and rescued cardiomyocyte differentiation efficiency with more cells presenting a polygonal or spindle-like shape (Figure 1P and Q).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from rescue experiments shown in Figure 1O.

claim: Exogenous SHH rescued cardiomyocyte differentiation efficiency with more cells presenting a polygonal or spindle-like shape.
source: It also up-regulated the expression of SHF markers ISL1 and MEF2C in D5 SORBS2-shRNA1 cells (Figure 1O) and rescued cardiomyocyte differentiation efficiency with more cells presenting a polygonal or spindle-like shape (Figure 1P and Q).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data from rescue experiments shown in Figure 1P-Q.

claim: About 40–60% Sorbs2-/- mice died within 1 week after birth.
source: In a previous report, about 40–60% Sorbs2-/- mice died within 1 week after birth (Zhang et al., 2016), indicating a possible structural heart defect(s).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: 137 embryos at E18.5 were collected from Sorbs2 mutant breeding.
source: To this end, we collected 137 embryos at E18.5.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: The ratio of genotype distribution among E18.5 embryos was consistent with Mendel's law.
source: The ratio of genotype distribution among embryos was consistent with Mendel's law (Supplementary file 3), suggesting no embryo loss in early development stage.
evidence: This claim is supported by genotype distribution data shown in Supplementary file 3.

claim: There was no embryo loss in early development stage in Sorbs2 mutants.
source: The ratio of genotype distribution among embryos was consistent with Mendel's law (Supplementary file 3), suggesting no embryo loss in early development stage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that genotype distribution follows Mendel's law.

claim: None of 30 dissected Sorbs2-/- embryos showed conotruncal defect or ventricular septal defect.
source: We dissected 30 Sorbs2-/- embryos, and none of them showed conotruncal defect or ventricular septal defect (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: About 40% (12/30) Sorbs2-/- hearts had atrial septal defect (ASD).
source: However, we found that about 40% (12/30) Sorbs2-/- hearts had atrial septal defect (ASD) with 10 being the absence/hypoplaisa of primary septum and two being double atrial septum (DAS) (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2C and data in Supplementary file 3.

claim: 10 out of 12 Sorbs2-/- hearts with ASD had absence/hypoplasia of primary septum.
source: However, we found that about 40% (12/30) Sorbs2-/- hearts had atrial septal defect (ASD) with 10 being the absence/hypoplaisa of primary septum and two being double atrial septum (DAS) (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2C and data in Supplementary file 3.

claim: 2 out of 12 Sorbs2-/- hearts with ASD had double atrial septum (DAS).
source: However, we found that about 40% (12/30) Sorbs2-/- hearts had atrial septal defect (ASD) with 10 being the absence/hypoplaisa of primary septum and two being double atrial septum (DAS) (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2C and data in Supplementary file 3.

claim: The penetrance of ASD in Sorbs2-/- mice is similar to the ratio of reported postnatal lethality.
source: The penetrance of ASD is similar to the ratio of reported postnatal lethality, indicating that ASD might contribute to early postnatal death.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of ASD penetrance with previously reported postnatal lethality.

claim: ASD might contribute to early postnatal death in Sorbs2-/- mice.
source: The penetrance of ASD is similar to the ratio of reported postnatal lethality, indicating that ASD might contribute to early postnatal death.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the correlation between ASD penetrance and postnatal lethality.

claim: A major part of atrial septum is derived from dorsal mesenchyme protrusion (DMP) originated from posterior SHF.
source: A major part of atrial septum is derived from dorsal mesenchyme protrusion (DMP) originated from posterior SHF (Kelly, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: 5 out of 15 E10.5 Sorbs2-/- embryos had DMP malformation.
source: We also noted DMP malformation in 5 out of 15 E10.5 Sorbs2-/- embryos.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The majority of Sorbs2-/- embryos with DMP malformation had DMP aplasia/hypoplasia (n = 4).
source: The majority of them had DMP aplasia/hypoplasia (n = 4), whereas one of them had duplicated DMP (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: One Sorbs2-/- embryo had duplicated DMP.
source: The majority of them had DMP aplasia/hypoplasia (n = 4), whereas one of them had duplicated DMP (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The dichotomy of DMP morphology is consistent with two opposite ASD phenotypes seen in E18.5 embryos.
source: The dichotomy of DMP morphology is consistent with two opposite ASD phenotypes seen in E18.5 embryos.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of both hypoplastic and duplicated DMP corresponding to different ASD phenotypes.

claim: The in vivo phenotype of Sorbs2-/- mice supports that SORBS2 haploinsufficiency in 4q deletion contributes to CHD pathogenesis through affecting SHF development.
source: Overall, the in vivo phenotype of Sorbs2-/- mice further supports that SORBS2 haploinsufficiency in 4q deletion contributes to CHD pathogenesis through affecting SHF development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mouse model data showing ASD and DMP defects.

claim: Sorbs2 is highly expressed in cardiomyocytes and in a subgroup of cardiac progenitors that also express Isl1 and Tbx1.
source: We identified nine subgroups as cardiac progenitors or cardiomyocytes and noted that Sorbs2 is highly expressed in cardiomyocytes and in a subgroup of cardiac progenitors that also express Isl1 and Tbx1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Three out of four Notch and Shh signaling target genes (Hey1, Heyl, and Ptch1) were significantly down-regulated in E10.5 Sorbs2-/- embryos.
source: Consistent with hESC differentiation results, we detected significantly down-regulated expression in three out of four Notch and Shh signaling target genes (Hey1, Heyl, and Ptch1) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Multivariate PERMANOVA revealed a significant combined difference in Notch and Shh signaling target expression between wild-type and Sorbs2-/- embryos (p<0.009).
source: Multivariate PERMANOVA (permutational multivariate analysis of variance) revealed a significant combined difference in Notch and Shh signaling target expression between wild-type and Sorbs2-/- embryos (p<0.009).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of qPCR data.

claim: Wild-type embryos are clustered together in PCA analysis of RNA-seq data.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) indicates that wild-type embryos are clustered together, whereas Sorbs2-/- embryos are more scattered (±), which is consistent with diverged cardiac phenotypes of Sorbs2-/- embryos.
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Sorbs2-/- embryos are more scattered in PCA analysis of RNA-seq data.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) indicates that wild-type embryos are clustered together, whereas Sorbs2-/- embryos are more scattered (±), which is consistent with diverged cardiac phenotypes of Sorbs2-/- embryos.
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The scattered distribution of Sorbs2-/- embryos in PCA is consistent with diverged cardiac phenotypes.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) indicates that wild-type embryos are clustered together, whereas Sorbs2-/- embryos are more scattered (±), which is consistent with diverged cardiac phenotypes of Sorbs2-/- embryos.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between PCA distribution and phenotypic variation.

claim: The majority of Sorbs2+/- samples are juxtaposed more closely to Sorbs2-/- embryos in PCA plot.
source: Interestingly, the majority of Sorbs2+/- samples are juxtaposed more closely to Sorbs2-/- embryos in PCA plot, indicating a molecular phenotype in heterozygous mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There is a molecular phenotype in Sorbs2+/- heterozygous mutants.
source: Interestingly, the majority of Sorbs2+/- samples are juxtaposed more closely to Sorbs2-/- embryos in PCA plot, indicating a molecular phenotype in heterozygous mutants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PCA clustering pattern of heterozygous samples.

claim: Genes significantly down-regulated in Sorbs2+/- heterozygous mutants are enriched in pathways involved in muscle development and embryonic morphogenesis.
source: We selected genes significantly down-regulated in heterozygous mutants (log2(fold change)>0.25, p<0.05) to perform GO analysis and found that these genes are enriched in pathways involved in muscle development and embryonic morphogenesis (Figure 3C, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 3C and Supplementary file 4.

claim: Genes significantly down-regulated in Sorbs2-/- homozygous mutants are enriched in pathways regulating heart development, myofibril assembly, and cardiac septum development.
source: Using the same threshold, we selected genes significantly down-regulated in homozygous mutants to perform GO analysis. These genes are enriched in pathways regulating heart development, myofibril assembly, and cardiac septum development (Figure 3D, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 3D and Supplementary file 5.

claim: The Notch signaling pathway was in the enrichment list of down-regulated genes in Sorbs2-/- homozygous mutants.

claim: A portion of Sorbs2-/- embryos had obvious down-regulation of Notch and Shh signaling targets.

claim: Down-regulation of Notch and Shh signaling targets in a portion of Sorbs2-/- embryos is consistent with a low penetrance of ASD in homozygous mutants.
source: A portion of embryos had obvious down-regulation of Notch and Shh signaling targets (Figure 3I), which is consistent with a low penetrance of ASD in homozygous mutants.

claim: Rare genetic variants play a significant role in CHD occurrence.

claim: The targeted panel includes 23 candidate CNV genes containing SORBS2 and 81 known CHD genes from literature.
source: Besides 23 candidate CNV genes containing SORBS2, the targeted panel also includes 81 known CHD genes from literature.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Targeted sequencing was performed on 300 complex CHD cases (two cases removed due to low-quality data).
source: Targeted sequencing was performed on 300 complex CHD cases (two cases removed due to low-quality data).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: 220 Han Chinese descents from the 1000 genome project were used as controls.
source: 220 Han Chinese descents from the 1000 genome project were used as controls.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The ethnicity of CHD and control groups was matched by PCA.

claim: 43.57% (n = 369) of 847 nonsynonymous variants had a minor allele frequency (MAF) below 1% across ExAC database and were adjudicated as 'damaging' by at least two algorithms.
source: Of the 847 nonsynonymous variants, 43.57% (n = 369) variants had a minor allele frequency (MAF) below 1% across ExAC database and were adjudicated as 'damaging' by at least two algorithms (PolyPhen2, SIFT, or MutationTaster).
evidence: This is a description of the variant filtering and classification results.

claim: 4 out of 57 genes (SORBS2, KMT2D, EVC2, and SH3PXD2B) had a p-value lower than 0.05 in gene-based Fisher's exact test.
source: 4 out of 57 genes (SORBS2, KMT2D, EVC2, and SH3PXD2B) had a p-value lower than 0.05 (one-tailed Fisher's exact) and two of them (SORBS2 and KMT2D) had a statistically significant mutation burden after the correction for multiple testing (q<0.20) (Figure 4B, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4B and Supplementary file 7.

claim: Two genes (SORBS2 and KMT2D) had a statistically significant mutation burden after the correction for multiple testing (q<0.20).
source: 4 out of 57 genes (SORBS2, KMT2D, EVC2, and SH3PXD2B) had a p-value lower than 0.05 (one-tailed Fisher's exact) and two of them (SORBS2 and KMT2D) had a statistically significant mutation burden after the correction for multiple testing (q<0.20) (Figure 4B, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4B and Supplementary file 7.

claim: KMT2D is a well-known CHD gene.

claim: Rare SORBS2 variants have similar levels of enrichment in CHDs as the known CHD genes.

claim: The distribution of rare SORBS2 damaging variants in CHD patients spread throughout the gene.

claim: Missense mutations identified in the CHD cohort caused protein aggregation in cells.

claim: Missense mutations in SORBS2 suggest an abnormal function of these variant proteins.
source: Although we didn't detect SORBS2 nonsense variants in CHD patients, missense mutations identified in our cohort caused protein aggregation in cells (Figure 4D), suggesting an abnormal function of these variant proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of protein aggregation.

claim: A high prevalence (85%, 17/20) of ASD was observed in patients carrying SORBS2 variants.
source: A high prevalence (85%, 17/20) of ASD, the defect seen in Sorbs2-/- hearts, was observed in patients carrying SORBS2 variants (Supplementary file 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by patient phenotype data shown in Supplementary file 9.

claim: There is a significant enrichment of SORBS2 rare damaging variants in patients with ASD (17 out of 183 ASD patients versus 3 out of 117 non-ASD patients, p=0.0306).
source: In our CHD cohort, we noted a significant enrichment of SORBS2 rare damaging variants in patients with ASD (17 out of 183 ASD patients versus 3 out of 117 non-ASD patients, p=0.0306, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of variant distribution among different CHD subtypes.

claim: The common CHDs in 4q deletion syndrome include ASD, ventricular septal defect (VSD), pulmonary stenosis/atresia, and tetralogy of Fallot.
source: The common CHDs in 4q deletion syndrome include ASD, ventricular septal defect (VSD), pulmonary stenosis/atresia, and tetralogy of Fallot and so on Strehle and Bantock, 2003; Lin et al., 1988.

claim: The affected structures in 4q deletion syndrome CHDs are atrial septum and cardiac outflow tract, which are all derived from SHF.
source: The affected structures are atrial septum and cardiac outflow tract, which are all derived from SHF (Kelly, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: SORBS2 functions as a sarcomeric component to maintain cardiomyocyte function.
source: Indeed, our data revealed that SORBS2 functions not only as a sarcomeric component to maintain cardiomyocyte function, but also as an adaptor protein to promote SHF progenitor commitment in in vitro cardiomyocyte differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed sarcomeric disruption in SORBS2-knockdown cells.

claim: SORBS2 functions as an adaptor protein to promote SHF progenitor commitment in in vitro cardiomyocyte differentiation.
source: Indeed, our data revealed that SORBS2 functions not only as a sarcomeric component to maintain cardiomyocyte function, but also as an adaptor protein to promote SHF progenitor commitment in in vitro cardiomyocyte differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed decrease in SHF markers and the role of SORBS2 in signaling pathways.

claim: ASD is detected in Sorbs2-/- mouse hearts.

claim: Sorbs2 regulates SHF development in vivo.
source: It supports that Sorbs2 regulates SHF development in vivo and its role is conserved across species.

claim: The role of Sorbs2 in SHF development is conserved across species.
source: It supports that Sorbs2 regulates SHF development in vivo and its role is conserved across species.
evidence: This is an inference based on similar findings in both human and mouse models.

source: Notch signaling promotes Smo accumulation in cilia and enhances cellular response to Shh, placing Notch upstream of Shh signaling (Stasiulewicz et al., 2015; Kong et al., 2015).

source: Therefore, SORBS2 might promote SHF progenitor fate through c-ABL/NOTCH/SHH axis.

source: It is likely that in vitro cardiomyocyte differentiation is a simplified model that cannot fully recapitulate the in vivo spatial and temporal information of various cardiac progenitors and, therefore, has less regulatory layers in which TBX5 may predominantly function as an FHF regulator.

claim: The penetrance of ASD in Sorbs2-/- mice is only 40%.

claim: SORBS2 has a relatively small effect in CHD pathogenesis.
source: Unlike human 4q deletion patients, Sorbs2-/- mice have no conotruncal defect and the penetrance of ASD is only 40%, indicating a relatively small effect of SORBS2 in CHD pathogenesis.
